claims.text: SCF 2025 Table 2 (thousands of 2025 $), median net worth 2022 to 2025: all 211.1 to 215.9 (SE 8.2, 6.4); under 35 42.7 to 33.0; 35-44 148.4 to 155.6; 45-54 270.6 to 253.7; 55-64 398.9 to 411.9; 65-74 448.6 to 431.3; 75+ 367.3 to 504.9; no HS diploma 41.6 to 18.6; HS 116.9 to 106.7; some college 149.3 to 181.0; college degree 508.5 to 505.4. Race medians White 311.9 to 332.1, Black 49.1 to 36.8, Hispanic 67.4 to 79.6, Asian 586.6 to 677.6; means White 1,694.7, Black 242.4 (2025)

SCF 2025: report says statistical significance 'generally is not addressed'; subgroup standard errors not in the bulletin; stock ownership direct or indirect 58% (2022) to 56% (2025), decline driven by families outside top 10% of income; direct 21% to 19%; homeownership 66.1% to 65.6%; top-decile median net worth $4,935.2k (2025); report finds 'little change in wealth inequality between surveys'
DFA covers 1989Q3 to most recent quarter; groups top 0.1%, next 0.9%, next 9%, next 40%, bottom half; page last updated 18 Sept 2026
Top 1% share of household net worth 32.5% in 2026Q2 (DFA release 18 Sept 2026), record; 31.7% in 2026Q1; series low 22.4% in 1990Q3; Fed restates history each release
Bottom 50% share of net worth 2.3% in 2026Q2 (2.4% a year earlier); 3.5% in 1989Q3; high 4.1% 1992Q3; low 0.4% 2010Q4-2012Q1 (DFA via FRED WFRBSB50215)
TheStreet (Apr 2026) citing Fed data: top 10% hold more than 87% of corporate equity and mutual fund shares; top 1% share 31.7% in 2025Q3 (earlier vintage)

Fed 2019 SCF note: 2019 medians White $188.2k, Black $24.1k (bounds 19.8-28.4), Hispanic $36.1k; median change 2007-10 White -27.3%, Black -27.7%, Hispanic -26.5%; 2010-13 White +1.4%, Black -23.0%, Hispanic -20.9%; 2013-16 W +16.7 B +25.7 H +45.2; 2016-19 W +3.5 B +32.6 H +64.9; homeownership under 35: White 46%, Black 17%, Hispanic 28%

Pew (SIPP): median household net worth 2005 to 2009 (2009 $): White 134,992 to 113,149 (-16%); Black 12,124 to 5,677 (-53%); Hispanic 18,359 to 6,325 (-66%); Asian 168,103 to 78,066 (-54%); 2005 home equity share of net worth Hispanic ~two-thirds, Black 59%, White 44%; zero/negative net worth 2009 Black 35%, Hispanic 31%, White 15%; main driver falling house values; Hispanics concentrated in CA, FL, NV, AZ

ad12_inherit.topic: Inheritance, estate tax, step-up in basis, buy-borrow-die

claims.text: Richmond Fed (SCF 2019, born 1949-72): received any transfer White 34.8%, Black 13.2%; mean if positive $303,100 vs $154,260; median $100,830 vs $74,460; nearly one-third of white recipients got multiple transfers vs 7%; ~5% of white recipients $1m+, virtually no Black; at least half of recipients get first transfer after age 40; 2019 medians $180,400 vs $20,700 (nearly 9x); prior estimates: inheritances 10-20% of gap (1997), transfers 26% (2020 simulation)

Boston Fed (Thompson and Sabelhaus 2023): transfers explain 14% of white-Black gap without controls; lifetime earnings, pension assets and human capital explain 80%; about one-third of white and 1 in 10 Black families receive any inheritance; more than half of inheritances/gifts under $50,000

CRS: estate tax exemption $675,000 and top rate 55% in 2001; $3.5m and 45% by 2009; 2010 repeal year with carryover-basis option, then $5m/35% (P.L. 111-312); ATRA 2013 permanent, 40%, $5m indexed; TCJA doubled 2018-2025 ($13.99m in 2025); P.L. 119-21 sets $15m from 2026 indexed, rate 40%

CRS: taxable estates 5,467 (0.21% of deaths) in 2016, 2,129 (0.07%) in 2019; share of decedents paying fell from 2.1% in 2001; FY2023 revenue $32bn (0.7% of federal revenue); top 10% by income pay 90%, top 1% 65%, top 0.1% 29%; 60% of returns over filing threshold paid no tax in 2019, mainly marital deduction; about 300 business/farm estates taxed

CRS step-up: stock bought $100,000, worth $200,000 at death, sold $250,000: heir taxed on $50,000; the $100,000 accrued in life 'never taxed'; under carryover basis gain would be $150,000; CBO: carryover basis would raise $7.2bn FY2024 rising to $26.6bn FY2032; in 2010 carryover elections, 43.6% of estate value was unrealized gain; arguments for and against summarised

Yale Budget Lab: buy-borrow-die 'a tax planning technique which allows wealthy Americans to pay low tax rates on consumed income'; loan proceeds work like sale proceeds without tax; Liscow and Fox: borrowing 1% of income of top 0.1% by net worth; borrowing 'a relatively minor source of cash income' in aggregate; reform options raise $102bn-$147bn over ten years

NTU Foundation (Wilford 2021): concedes 'a tax avoidance strategy that some wealthy individuals use', 'not foolproof', borrowing costs interest; argues US taxes income not paper wealth and rejects wealth tax / taxing loans

ProPublica: 25 richest Americans' wealth grew $401bn 2014-18 (Forbes), they paid $13.6bn federal income tax, 'true tax rate' 3.4% (taxes / wealth growth, ProPublica's own measure); phrase 'buy, borrow, die' attributed to USC law professor Edward McCaffery; Ellison credit line secured by ~$10bn of shares (2014 Oracle disclosure); typical household paid ~14% of income

ad12_2008.topic: 2008: subprime pricing, DOJ settlements, foreclosures, wealth loss, TARP

claims.text: DOJ: Wells Fargo settlement 12 July 2012, more than $175m in relief including $50m direct down-payment assistance; alleged ~4,000 African-American and Hispanic wholesale borrowers steered into subprime 2004-08 while similar white borrowers got prime, and ~30,000 charged higher fees and rates 2004-09; 'second largest fair lending settlement in the department's history'; allegations, release records no admission

DOJ: Countrywide (Bank of America subsidiary) $335m, 21 Dec 2011, largest residential fair lending settlement; alleged more than 200,000 African-American and Hispanic borrowers paid higher fees and rates 2004-08 than similar white borrowers; 'thousands' steered to subprime 2004-07; Holder: judgments should rest on 'creditworthiness, not on the color of their skin'

Bayer-Ferreira-Ross: seven metros 2004-07, credit-repository data; with credit score and risk controls, Black and Hispanic buyers 105% and 78% more likely to have high-cost purchase mortgages; 60-65% from sorting across lenders, 35-40% from differential treatment within lenders; concentrated at high-risk lenders

CRL Lost Ground 2011: of loans made 2004-08, 2.7m households had lost homes to foreclosure; ~1 in 4 Black and Hispanic borrowers foreclosed or seriously delinquent vs ~12% white; higher-income borrowers lost homes: Black 10%, Hispanic 15%, white 4.6%; 3.6m more at serious risk

CBO final TARP report (19 Apr 2024): $700bn authorised, $444bn disbursed (about $410bn by Mar 2011), estimated subsidy cost $31bn, driven largely by foreclosure-prevention grant programs, AIG and auto aid; transactions with other financial institutions yielded a net gain; last investment repaid Sept 2023
